The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate. Our analysis demonstrates that these phase plates can be configured to compensate for spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes, even at extremely low electron beam currents, yielding an theoretical potential for diffraction-limited performance. The alternative approach of using sophisticated solenoidal vector phase plates to achieve similar results is found to be infeasible due to high time-dependent ellipticity and astigmatism. In contrast, the phase plates can be set up to correct for spherical aberration with minimal time-dependent distortion. The solutions to these issues can be achieved down to electron beam currents of 10^-5 Ampere. The correctness of these assertions has been validated through numerical computation.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on either finding their decay products or their kernel. However, for certain rare decays, such as $B^+ \to K^+ E\!/$, where a invisible particle is emitted, only the missing energy can be used for identification, as the particle has no visible decay products. In this investigation, we examine the possibility of detecting axion-like particles through this type of rare decay. Using approximately 50$ \, \text{ab}^{-1}$ of data, we can investigate axion-like particles with a mass up to 1.85 GeV/$c^2$ and a recoil energy of less than 2.0 GeV/$c$ by using only missing energy to identify them in Belle II experiments, resulting in an expected overall signal efficiency of 13%.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, more frequently
than traditional static or non-contextualized approaches. We offer several
explanations for this contextual over-prioritization of semantic change and
propose an experiment to validate the most plausible one.

The Sgr A* at the center of the Milky Way and over 300 other AGN at the centers of galaxy bulges are believed to be powered by black holes. Every one of these massive black holes has the capacity to rotate, and in due course, general relativity dictates that they will spin and then lose energy through their own electromagnetic radiation in a characteristic pattern that can be identified in their distant spectral signatures. We will: 1) examine the feasibility of being able to accurately measure every black hole's own spin and mass in the near future, 2) review the constraints that scientists have already placed on the mass and spin of the most prominent black hole at the closest distance, and in the process gain a clearer understanding of the challenges and opportunities for a future that can be be able to accurately measure spin in a distant galaxy.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the oscillation of cell nuclei between the superficial and deep layers of the neuroepithelial tissue, also known as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM). Despite its significance, the underlying mechanisms driving this process are not fully understood. We utilized confocal microscopes to capture three-dimensional time-lapse images and machine learning to develop a workflow that segments migrating nuclei, tracks their paths, and computes their positions, velocities, and accelerations. By applying this approach to live tissue samples, we discovered that nuclei primarily move along specific axial paths with varying velocities in different tissue layers. Our proposed method provides a versatile and adaptable framework for analyzing the dynamic behavior of migrating nuclei within three-dimensional living tissue specimens.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately so automatically verifying the authenticity of ID cards has become a pressing need.  The primary goal of this project is to validate ID cards efficiently by integrating computer vision and natural language processing.  To achieve this, a system was developed that utilizes Tesseract for Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to convert ID card images into text, followed by manual verification to ensure the accuracy of the converted text.  Furthermore, an advanced version of this system was created using regular expressions to automatically check the formatted data extracted through the OCR process.  This system is valuable for confirming the authenticity of various ID cards and plays a crucial role in security measures to prevent unauthorised access.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational state of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids eventually reaches a stable equilibrium where the YORP effect can no longer restrain their rotation, potentially leading to rotational disruption or the breakup of more massive asteroids. Scholars speculate that this effect is responsible for small asteroids that possess extremely rapid rotation periods or irregular, low-mass asteroids with rotational periods equal to that of their parent body. To investigate the YORP effect's influence on these extreme asteroids, researchers utilized a numerical model based on the Discrete Ordinates Method to simulate radiation transfer and calculate the forces and torques exerted upon them. As a result of this analysis, it was discovered that ten percent of the asteroids in the sample list (2009 TC 6, 2008 TC21, and 2010 SO) are likely to be spun up to extreme rates as a result of the YORP effect, whereas, for the majority of the studied asteroids, other factors such as mass redistribution, geological activity, or impacts are believed to be more influential than the YORP effect in shaping their rotational behavior.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some of these models can perform tasks that are not computably continuous. This paper proves that the class of functions definable by single-pass, singly incremental transducers is precisely those that are computably continuous and can be expressed using rational equations. This relationship is also equivalent to a subset of regular functions that are computably continuous. Furthermore, we identify a specific two-way transducer format called RNTI, and demonstrate that any system of rational equations is consistent if and only it represents all outputs achievable by an RNTI-transducer. This relationship can also be compared to a subformat of RNTI.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems and requires a significantly shorter training period by utilizing a simpler-to-train simulation of the system. The recent advancement of reservoir computing enables the use of vast amounts of real-world data for training, while maintaining a smaller projection of the state variables compared to traditional methods. A key benefit of the new approach is its ability to accurately forecast time series with minimal training data, even as it leverages larger datasets. A 32-system simulation of a Baos-91 weather predictor time series demonstrates that the new technique can accurately forecast complex time series with a significantly shorter training period and a more efficient projection of state variables.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy forms a gradient rather than distinct categories. Numerous studies have demonstrated the VTC's response differences to living and non-living entities or specific points along the spectrum, but two key hypotheses explain these findings. The first hypothesis, a shared-hypersurface, suggests that the cortex encodes shared features between visual inputs and visual-conceptual inputs along certain axes, including the animacy spectrum. The second hypothesis, an entity-separation, proposes that visual inputs occupy distinct regions of population activity for the entire range from simple shapes to complex living beings. Utilizing population-recoding techniques and functional imaging, our study found support for the shared-hypersurface hypothesis through tests of axis invariance, regression analysis, and rotation invariance. Additionally, we believe our analysis methods can be applied to other complex sensory-domain continuums.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect on program performance.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases through digital communication channels like WhatsApp and Facebook has significantly exacerbated global outbreaks. These events, known as super-spreader events, are responsible for a disproportionate amount of new infections and have been linked to the difficulty in containing diseases like COVID-19. Despite their evident impact, research into their underlying mechanisms and integration into mathematical models for transmission remain limited. In this context, we propose a novel framework where transmission dynamics are modeled using time-varying $R_0$ values that change in response to observable factors, including an innovative idea of random "super-spreading" events. By introducing a time-dependent network formed from a static backbone through instantaneous links, we demonstrate that our model can replicate the effects of super-spreading events statistically. Furthermore, we develop an approach to infer the probability distribution of effective $R_0$ values from empirical data. When applied to secondary infection data from a time-varying network, our model reveals that a few events with high effective $R_0$ values are responsible for the majority of infections, accurately reflecting the characteristics observed in actual data.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to build upon the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially defined for a specific type of operator within L(X), by introducing and examining the codiskcyclic nature of shift operators associated with a specific class of weighted sequence spaces, denoted as $w^\alpha$, where $w^\alpha$ consists of all sequences x = (x_n) of scalars such that the sequence y = (\alpha^n x_n) is absolutely summable, for some given sequence of positive real numbers $\alpha$. We will then go on to investigate and characterize the codiskcyclicity of these weighted backward shift operators.

The paper addresses the problem of component vector magnetic field estimation along the sight line from the Sun through analyses of state-of-the-art inversion techniques, atmospheric modeling methods, and data inversion. It examines major sources of error, such as atmospheric model limitations and data inversion constraints, and highlights recent research relevant to future instruments designed for state-of-the-site data measurement. It also reviews current and upcoming instruments, analyzing their biases and precisions for component vector measurement. A summary of biases in magnetic field components, particularly in the smaller component, is provided with associated references. It also provides a list of suggestions to reduce bias in the component vector magnetic field estimation.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X doesn't share the same asymptotic behavior as p_Y. As a result, intrinsic complexity, defined where p_X equals p_Y for all equivalent subshifts equivalent to X, cannot typically be decided.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34,414 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast dataset from the APOGEE-2. The study involved using a two-component model to break down elemental abundances into supernovae types II and I, and was informed by theoretical stellar evolution and globular cluster data. The model revealed significant correlations with specific ratios of stars, and we found that a mixture of elliptical orbits and a spin-orbit disk accurately represented the observed distribution of stars. The study also found that the stellar disk is more populated with types II supernovae remnants in its inner regions, while its outer regions resemble the globular cluster system with an 'old' population. This difference is associated with the two types of supernovae and could have implications for dark matter detection. The study involved analyzing large datasets and produced a vast amount of information on the composition of stars in the Milky Way disk.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020, exacerbating situations with rumors disseminated socially, and motivating the need to address the relationship between them. This study examined the spatial spread of the "COVID dies in you" rumor on Weibo from May to June 2020, and used the Google Knowledge Graph to categorize the rumor's audience by profession, location, and related keywords. A significant correlation was found between the keyword distribution of the rumor's audience and the COVID-19 pandemic's high incidence areas, indicating that information spread is influenced by disease transmission patterns. Furthermore, this research found that the rumor's and pandemic's spread exhibited similar temporal patterns with a cross-correlation of 0.829, and that high incidence provinces played a more crucial role in information spread than low incidence provinces. A coupled dynamics model was developed to analyze the mutual influence between information spread and disease transmission, and the model's cross effects were examined.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets from multiple hosts. We have obtained comprehensive catalogs of likely planetary nebulae in just two relatively close galaxies, Andromeda and M33, utilizing existing archival materials and previously published data on the positions of the nebulae. By combining existing spectral information with newly acquired spectra for each nebula, we have been able to determine the DNEb of each nebula in order to establish the distance to the galaxies through the method of法式星团. Our findings have resulted in estimated distances to the galaxies of 2.35 megaparsecs for Andromeda and 8.44 megaparsecs for M33, with associated uncertainties of 0.12 and 0.34 megaparsecs respectively.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing semantic features and optimizations tailored to medical data, including optimized handling of missing values, relaxed data integrity assumptions, and optimized join operations. Furthermore, LifeStream incorporates safety mechanisms such as secure time synchronization, virus protection, and precise latency control. Our experiments in various scenarios, involving benchmarks and real-world cases, show that LifeStream outperforms other systems and manually programmed solutions by up to two orders of magnitude in terms of processing speed, while also offering a reliable and accurate platform for physiological data processing in clinical settings.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function is widely considered a key factor in the effective training of deep neural networks for supervised classification.  However, due to the availability of simple, high-performing baseline algorithms with default loss functions, a thorough examination of this issue has been limited.  In contrast, we present thorough comparative studies of commonly used loss functions across various benchmark datasets and image classification tasks, employing both shallow and deep neural network configurations.  In basic gradient descent-based training settings, we found that the performance gains from state-of-the-art attention mechanisms and graph-based co-training algorithms are consistently matched by a basic fully connected neural network using the Kullback-Leibler divergence as its loss function.  In addition, we discovered that the network's structure significantly influences the suitability of certain distance metrics, potentially explaining the conflicting findings reported in previous studies.  As the we investigate further into the impact of loss functions, we uncover multiple avenues for research that could lead to significant advancements.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, a coupled model of thermomechanics is necessary. Although existing unified models are available, they currently lack the capability to simulate the resulting thermal effects. A novel multifield extended phase-field model is thus developed to capture the interaction between mechanics and thermal effects in polymer deformation and crystallization processes. This proposed model is based on a comprehensive free energy density that incorporates both mechanical and thermal contributions. This free energy density is then used to derive the corresponding balance laws of mass and momentum as well as the second law of thermodynamics. Furthermore, a diffuse interface heat conduction model is proposed as described by the classical parabolic heat equation. The proposed model is thus established with five coupled nonlinear partial differential equations that are extensively studied using both analytical and numerical approaches. This includes a linear stability analysis of the steady-state solution, determination of the spinodal curve through the most-unstable mode analysis and a numerical solution using the fully implicit finite element method. The proposed model is thus established with several innovative features that include the consideration of both mechanical and thermal influences in phase-field evolution as well as the free-energy density formulation that influences both the mechanical and thermal properties of the polymer. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this study is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied two-dimensional magnetic field, which induces a $U(1)$ rotation in the two components of the spin-polarized order parameter's $\bf k$-space distribution. As a result, the magnetic susceptibility is found to be anisotropic and specifically, the Ginzburg-Landau calculations indicate that the magnetic susceptibility is significantly higher in the face of the topological surface compared to the bulk topological surface.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure's branch and state components are expanded to match the K*2$\mathcal{M}$-1 dimension. An optimized design is introduced by integrating a minimum Euclidean distance criterion with decision-based even symbol phasing and current symbol duration power spectral density analysis. This approach allows for significant signal-to-noise ratio gains over the conventional method, while also considering spectral efficiency. The proposed optimized schemes with two delays of one and two symbol durations are demonstrated for 4-Mary CPM modulation.

A previously reported finding from the research of the 1990s and 2000s is the strikingly uniform value of the ratio of variations to the mean in the energy density of quantum fields across various spacetime settings. Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue is re-examined using the Kosterlitz-Jaynes-Anderson (KJA) approach to quantum thermodynamics, leading to the conclusion that this result stems from the applicability of the 2-point stress-energy tensor correlator in only a limited range of high-energy conditions. Consequently, a broader comprehension of the result is gained by analyzing the meaning of KJA approach's thermodynamic quantities, particularly in relation to the free energy density, specific heat, and temperature variations.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require significant capital outlays. By leveraging a newly proposed hybrid objective function and utilizing the exponentially faster HHL quantum algorithm for portfolio rebalancing, these institutions could potentially save millions that are currently wasted. However, the HHL algorithm's impracticality stems from its requirement to perform a state-swapping operation, necessitating an impossible level of quantum coherence. To circumvent this obstacle, we propose a modified objective function devoid of the state-swapping requirement, thus making sub-exponential time portfolio rebalancing achievable and realistic.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the sampling rate adaptation of the attention mechanism with a consistency constraint on the representations encoded by both encoders. This new method, termed Multi-Modal Attention with Consistency (MAwC), utilizes the attention mechanism in the reverse direction to adjust the interaction between the audio and text features, thereby achieving sampling rate adaptation and consistency learning simultaneously. The MAwC approach is simple to implement and provides an effective enhancement to ASR performance when trained on single-modal data and a significant improvement when trained on multi-modal data with unpaired text data.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. This technique allows for the emulation of complex atomic systems without higher-energy states and enables precise control over multi-photon processes and transport mechanisms with spatially defined precision. The study derives analytical expressions for inter-orbital coupling and verifies their accuracy through spatially precise surface profiling and spectral measurements.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow and droplets suspended in the air. These droplets are subject to sedimentation, evaporation, and surface re-deposition on the floor, complicating the task of modeling and simulating virus-laden aerosol transport. In an effort to better understand and address this issue, this study employs advanced numerical methods to investigate the effects of speaking and breathing on the distribution of aerosols in a model bus. Using the large eddy simulation technique, we accurately captured the complex airflow patterns and acoustical forces generated by a speaker's mouth. By integrating the dispersion of aerosols with boundary conditions that account for their behavior on surfaces, this study provides high-resolution maps of airborne and suspended virus-laden particles. The results of this study offer new insights and practical suggestions for minimizing the spread of viruses through speech and speech-related activities.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect, a phenomenon where Spin-Orbit Coupling is enhanced in a specific layer adjacent to a strong spin-orbit material interface, exhibits significant properties and potential applications in nanotechnology.  Recently, theories have explored the spin-orbit proximity effect within超導 and non-equilibrium contexts.  However, for Equilibrium scenarios, particularly those involving strong spin-orbit coupling, existing Understanding has been limited.  This paper aims to address this gap by deriving a general expression for the spin-orbit proximity effect within the Equilibrium framework, utilizing a self-consistent approach.  We employ a Taylor series expansion of the spin-orbit coupling, enabling an analytical analysis of TDM structures where the spin-orbit effect is present only on a single atom.  As a result, we investigate how various parameters influence the distribution of spin-orbit coupling in the adjacent molecule.  Our analysis highlights the critical role of phase and magnitude of orbital overlap in determining the behavior of the spin-orbit proximity effect, demonstrating an unusual phenomenon where the spin-orbit coupling may actually decrease in certain situations.  Our findings provide a detailed understanding of the mechanism behind the spin-orbit proximity effect, a generalizable knowledge applicable to a wide range of molecular structures.  We demonstrate our theory's applicability through a case study on a specific molecular structure, Pt-Al dimer, and verify our results through comparisons with numerical NDD calculations.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, impacts its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, which is suitable for practical applications. This approach considers the relationship between gradient norms and local Lipschitz constants, and we demonstrated it through an exact calculation. To better understand the connection, we conducted a series of experiments using our straightforward method to optimize a variable-transformed trained neural networks, with the aim of minimizing their upper bounds for a specified task. To this end, we employed the upper bound as a regularizer during training, and discovered that, in contrast to direct optimization of the Lipschitz constant, this method yielded significantly better results. Neural networks trained in this manner exhibited a considerable increase in generalization capabilities. This was evident when evaluating the impact of overfitting and when assessing smaller, previously unseen subsets of MNIST and CIFAR-10, where we observed the smallest drops in accuracy in comparison to other regularizers. We believe our straightforward approach to determining the upper bound has broader applications, and that regularizing the Lipschitz constant is an effective strategy to enhance neural networks' robustness and their ability to generalize.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies.

The Leslie Stephen Prize for Physics 2021 went to three physicists: David Dunbar Sonenberg, Per Lundqvist, and Norman S. Samardzijski for their groundbreaking work on precise calculations in positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. PET imaging relies on precise calculations of how positrons interact with matter after being emitted, but existing approximations in these calculations may have significant errors in certain scenarios. Such inaccuracies could have potential risks associated with sensitive populations, including patients who have had material implanted in their bodies, and could hinder the development of new applications for PET imaging. A full version of this abstract is available upon request.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates that these systems do recognize the coherence of a text in accordance with CT, particularly in terms of their preference for certain paths within the discourse. This finding is validated through additional experiments considering the complexity of statements and the use of semantic information.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements at unknown locations are gathered and mapped to specific positions, has become a standard approach in positioning. However, due to the inherent variability and variability of WiFi signals, simple and ineffective comparison methods are insufficient for creating accurate fingerprints. In this study, we explore the utilization of Machine-Learning-based signal processing to enhance the efficiency of matching and modeling based on a cost-effective, low-power testbed. To achieve this, we developed a compact and versatile testbed that allows for the precise comparison of signal variability using a low-cost hardware setup. To handle the issue of signal variability, we employ an autocorrelation-based signal processing method, which is easily implementable on low-power devices. Furthermore, in order to resolve the problem of variability and variability simultaneously, we investigate the use of Auto-Encoder based signal processing. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, we utilize a low-power testbed for indoor positioning with a WiFi fingerprint. To facilitate the creation of a scalable and efficient testbed that facilitates precise signal processing and indoor positioning, we discuss the design considerations of this setup in this study.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs.

In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit to provide this information. To achieve this, the calculation was performed in the NMRK limit of one another's kinematic configuration. To do so, various reductions were necessary, including the factorization of soft gluon emissions, the application of momentum conservation in hard jets, and the integration over one another's kinematics in a low rapidity interval. Theories describing polymer brushes coated on curved surfaces have provided significant insights into self-assembling blocks copolymer systems used in nanotechnology. However, these models fell short in accounting for the zone immediately adjacent to the curved surface, where polymer chains remain grafted without extending into a brush-like configuration. In this study, we develop a revised theoretical framework that incorporates this end exclusion zone by utilizing an entropic closure constraint within the self-consistent field framework. We test this model with substrates of constant curvature, revealing that it predicts enhanced symmetry in parabolic surfaces and characteristics of oscillatory brushing effects in cylindrical surfaces, now observed also in these curved environments.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emission patterns across the full sky. Furthermore, compared to standard interpolation, dictionary learning with additional training produced more accurate all-sky maps. The results demonstrate the potential of this approach for managing large datasets from upcoming gamma-ray telescopes like the Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach, which involves a limited number of action selections by individual agents. We find that for a wide variety of problem types, there exists an action selection approach using O(n^2) queries, which guarantees a combinatorial gap of at least 1/e from the optimal social welfare, in contrast to an unbounded combinatorial optimization social welfare gap when employing random action sequences. We also explore the impact of a natural budget constraint, which limits the number of actions an individual may select, and derive results on the combinatorial optimization social welfare attainable when employing a non-deterministic serial dictatorship approach. We further examine the impact of a stricter constraint, in which a previous agent's action selections are undisclosed to subsequent agents, and provide an algorithm achieving a budget approximation ratio of e - 1/epsilon with a natural budget constraint of 1/epsilon.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, as these 
binaries can provide valuable information about binary stability and 
asteroid masses. Initially, we processed individual frames from the ZTF 
database to create precise star positions and measurements, then monitored 
their positional relationships over time to identify potential binary 
associations. Subsequently, we examined these associations within a given 
probability range to determine their binaries' orbital parameters, periods, 
total masses, and separation distances. By doing so, we discovered ten 
binary asteroids with wide orbits cataloged in the Minor Planet Center, 
including (4769 Castalia/1988 SZ), (86 Semeke/2015 ZG1), and (1044 Geographos/2015 ZG1). Furthermore, our study offers general 
guidelines for evaluating binary discoveries in large-scale surveys, as 
well as the necessary conditions for detecting wide binaries effectively.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then uses these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This method highlights the importance of local features in the sequence of these protein structures. In contrast, another investigation employing another topological modeling approach finds that, in contrast to knotted proteins, the majority of unknotted proteins are folded into compact shapes. Furthermore, we observe that projections of X-ray crystallographic protein structures differ significantly from those folded into tight clusters. By analyzing the angles formed by three consecutive axes in 2D projections, we discover that most protein structures exhibit preferentially acute angles, in contrast to non-protein ring polymers, which display obtuse angles more frequently. This unexpected finding suggests that proteins are characterized by their elongated and flexible nature. In addition, we find that the crystallographic structures of proteins exhibit the same acute angle preference as simulated flexible polymers, in contrast to rigid polymer models, which are more likely to adopt dense, globular shapes. This surprising result once again underscores the exceptional elongated and flexible nature of most protein structures.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In examining the mechanism for the anomalous NG phenomenon, we utilized three distinct approaches - bracket generation, first-order symmetric metric geometry, and the concept of Lie group cosets. Through these analyses, we derived an expression for the anomalous NG theorem that in turn proves an altered Heisenberg uncertainty relation. In exploring altered Lie algebras, we were able to discover a direct correlation between the anomalous NG theorem and altered Heisenberg algebras. In examining altered geometry, we found that the lack of a well-defined position of an altered Lie group orbit directly contributes to the phenomenon of the anomalous NG theorem. In examining Lie groups, we demonstrated that the position of a specific closed Lie subgroup relative to its parent group can account for the anomalous NG theorem. In doing so, we found expressions for the anomalous NG theorem in terms of position, altered geometry, and altered Lie algebras, respectively. As a result of this research, we were able to generalize the anomalous NG theorem beyond its original mathematical framework. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are constrained when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a large language model to generate noisy natural comments in multiple areas, which are then used to create a pertinent generator that produces high-quality, large-scale counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. We demonstrate that applying this counterfactual data as a proxy auxiliary information in learning yields a robust model that yields a 2.22 average accuracy boost on unlabeled perturbed test sets from new devices, and a 5.51 accuracy gain on clean test sets when training with noisy natural comments is feasible.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene is gaining interest, yet definitive proof is lacking.  In our study, we investigated the remote epitaxial growth of InPtSn/Gr and AgCuGa/Cr/Gr structures, and found strong indications of remote epitaxy in certain cases.  Specifically, we detected the (111) crystallographic orientation in InPtSn and observed the Bragg-Rocherleigh condition in both the (111)-oriented AgCuGa and the cubic CuAlSn structures, which serve as strong evidence for remote epitaxy.  In addition, we discovered that a Bragg-Rocherleigh layer exists in the AgCuGa structure, and we believe this phenomenon may also occur in the CuAlSn structure.  Furthermore, we observed remote van der Waals layers in both the AgCuGa and CuAlSn structures.  In contrast, we found no such layers in the cubic CuAlSn structure or the tetragonal PdAlSb structure.  In the case of InPtSn, we detected two distinct growth modes, with a second mode exhibiting distinct features from the first. A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required.  This problem has limited real-world applications and makes collecting such data impossible in many instances.  To address this limitation, a novel single-label conditional GAN framework is proposed that automatically generates multi-label conditions without human intervention.  The proposed method employs a predictive network based GAN architecture, which requires only single-label training data, significantly simplifying the data annotation process.  This innovative approach is implemented and evaluated on synthetic and real image datasets, yielding a $0.19 Fr\'{e}chet$ distance improvement over the baseline conditional GAN results.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the activation of particles in jets or the core of these galaxies offers a compelling explanation for this phenomenon.  In our research, we propose a method to estimate the gamma-rays produced when protons in a jet smash into photons, generating a broad spectrum of high radiation across radio, optical, and gamma-rays bands.  Our proposed model accurately generates the observed broad spectrum of galaxies like 3C279 and 3C273 if the proton and electron populations interact via a 'compressive' process in the galaxies' low-energy jets.  It also allows us to infer the size of the interaction site, estimate the energy consumption of the jet, and determine the current energy consumption rate.  It is observed that the interaction site is situated within a specific distance range from the periphery of the light speed cylinder, and the galaxies' Hazy Sphere model accurately reproduces the characteristic broad spectrum of GeV gamma-rays and their cosmic ray contribution to low-energy radiation.  However, our model fails to account for the most energetic gamma-rays in the TeV range.
