This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the condition that the nonlinearity is $L^{2}$-subcritical in specific higher dimensional cases ($5 < d \le 9$), we find that all such solutions behave as if in an unbounded domain, never entering the obstacle. However, in a higher dimensional range ($d \ge 5$), solutions under the same conditions will eventually enter the obstacle and result in a singularity formation within a finite time period. We also provide an internal blow-up solution that remains within the obstacle at the moment of collapse.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. Our theorem 3.12 demonstrates that this system of vector bundles is equivalent to a category of symmetric n-tensors within the 2-fibred world. Our construction of the full linearisation has an extension to local theories and incorporates the definition of a symmetric graded local Lagrangian submanifold. Our theorem 4.7 establishes a one-to-one correspondence between symmetric n-tensor field automorphisms and symmetric graded local vector field automorphisms. Our final main theorem 4.12 demonstrates a similar correspondence for the 2-categories of symmetric local theories.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in driving scientific progress, but traditional point-based methods lack a Bayesian alternative for a key aspect of hypothesis testing. Researchers are currently exploring various approaches to fill this gap, including exploring the integration of H0 and H1 within a broader parametric framework. We outline several key elements that should be considered in such explorations, including the justification for employing Bayes factors under the assumption of continuous distributions, exploring appropriate hypotheses under the discrete case, and highlighting challenges in interpreting hypotheses within broader frameworks. We also outline open questions related to Bayes factor interpretation, exploring the relationship between hypotheses within broader frameworks, and exploring the relationship between Bayes factors and CIs within such contexts. Ultimately, this content serves as a foundation for further investigation into these complex issues.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and apply the Burer-Monteiro factorization technique to transform it into an unstructured rmdual problem. After identifying a specific geometric landscape for the Burer-Monteiro objective within the Riemannian quotient geometry of Stiefel matrices, we analyze three distinct regions: one where global minima are found, another containing stationary points with a specific value gradient, and a third region where stationary points with a perpendicular value gradient are located. We also prove that any solution with a specific value belongs to the first region and always resides in its respective region type within the second and third regions. These theoretical findings are validated through extensive numerical experiments on various psd semidefinite problems, including copymax, copsemimax, and tcsemnorm minimization.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to do so. Utilizing the simulation data, we identified key parameters influencing the system's ability to reach a Nash Equilibrium. Our results showed that the ability to infer peers' payoffs was critical, as learning that does not involve this transmission led to an inability of the population to converge on a Nash Equilibrium. Additionally, our social-learning models exhibited more propensity for oversimplification compared to individual learning, ultimately requiring the incorporation of random exploration to prevent this tendency.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word orderings across languages and beyond words, we also consider character-level information. This is made possible by analyzing the character profiles of words in each language's vocabulary space. Our method integrates three distinct signals through a clustering process. We assess the alignment of the character profiles using a proposed metric, and we apply the resulting constraints through an alignment procedure that preserves both character and word-level information. The results of an experimental study show that this approach significantly enhances performance when compared to the baseline methodology, particularly for languages with limited resources.

The initial production particle number ($dN_{ch}/d\eta$) is connected to the radial flow generated in high-energy collisions, as demonstrated by the use of the five-parameter Langevin model to fit various data sets of hadron yields. This model considers the mass of hadrons, as well as two key transverse-velocity parameters, together with the initial particle number and the transverse-momentum distribution. When applied to soft and intermediate soft data sets, the model effectively incorporates the influence of collective flow, as evidenced by its accurate replication of hadron ratio signs and mass dependence. The model also reflects the soft-sector color confinement mechanism, as evidenced by the absence of $c$-quark hadrons in its predictions. The model's assumptions are further supported by the absence of bose-enhancement in its predictions for open charm and beauty yields, as well as the absence of bottomonium decays. The model's limitations are acknowledged, including the lack of consideration for electromagnetic radiation, the radiation of heavy quarks, and the influence of flavor quantum numbers on hadron charges. The model's simplicity is acknowledged, including the assumption of an isotropic hadron distribution. The model's utility is acknowledged, including the ability to estimate charged-hadron momentum distributions and the initial production particle number from experimental data, as well as the ability to evaluate the hadronization of soft hadrons, $c$- and $b$-quarks, and top quarks. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this extended approach is character set-agnostic. We draw a connection to the logic known as ETRN with intersection and complement, establishing a containment solution based on ETRN with intersection and complement's query answer problem, providing a distinctive characteristic of these patterns that is uniform in the character set. However, demonstrating the approach's foundational nature proves challenging, as establishing a uniform framework with infinitely large character sets is not straightforward. Additionally, although a related pattern system was previously proposed, our research reveals its approach to containment problem resolution is ultimately flawed.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular, benefit from the use of factor graphs, which provide a structured representation for optimizing relationships between states and observations. One such application is in autonomous driving, and to support these applications, open-source datasets like Highway-Haven have been created. To test and enhance VIO models, researchers can rely on these datasets and existing algorithms, and through this research, a Python-based implementation of the factor-graph-based VIO algorithm is available.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, to illustrate our approach. As a result, we discover that this new model exhibits both higher-order Weyl semimetal and topological phoenex semimetal characteristics. Specifically, we show that the square root of a 3D crystal structure's Wyll semimetal hosts a Weyl point on its Brillouin zone boundary, while the square root of a 3D honeycomb Weyl semimetal model displays folded Weyl points within the Brilouin zone, effectively realising a higher-order Weyl semimetal state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that taking the square root of a Hamiltonian with Femi-Sea filling leads to a topological phoenix semimetal state. By using non-local order parameters, we effectively characterize these exotic phases. Our study also provides a general method for implementing such square-root Hamiltonians through photonic and ultracold atoms systems.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment. A non-iterative approach to quasi-reversibility is applied, and a discrete method using edge-based finite elements is developed. Stability analysis and a convergence estimate are derived, and this theory is validated through a computational example.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows for the efficient training of models in a federated environment. In this scenario, participants, whose data remains private, engage with a group of servers with varying levels of computational power to model development. This scenario is relevant to industries such as mobile banking, healthcare, and the Internet of Vehicles. We created an algorithm for FedSA on the FISS framework that leverages the capabilities of powerful servers while minimizing communication with them. This approach utilizes the strength of high-capacity servers to process complex calculations, taking into account an increasing number of bits per participant. We assess the efficiency of our algorithm in a practical setting, simulating the training of an XGBoost model for credit card default prediction using data from more than 50,000 customers.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions.

A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems. Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum from an infinite, memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories, our research finds its change in coarse-grained entropy to be directly proportional to the square root of an expression accounting for the average null energy flux and the corresponding change in incoming energy and momentum, which is then shown to be inherently connected to the quantum null energy condition. Furthermore, our research also reveals that an average null energy condition, widely regarded as a variant of the quantum null energy condition, is sufficient to prevent an increase in the quench-induced coarse-grained entropy, and is then shown to be equivalent to a specific bound on the quench-induced entropy per unit of incoming energy and momentum. Finally, our research also yields an analogous relationship between an average null energy condition and the modification of the Hubble constant in an expanding universe.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm.

Consider a unit cube $Q_n$ in $n$-dimensional space and a function space $C(Q_n)$ consisting of continuous functions, where the norm is defined as the maximum absolute value of a function. Now, let $\Sigma_n$ be the set of all $2^n$ corners of the cube $Q_n$. There exists a map that takes any set of $2^n$角点 in a way that preserves corner positions and function norms, which can be achieved through a combination of rotations, translations, and a constant value adjustment in a way that the difference between the highest and lowest values remains unchanged. If the function space is replaced with a larger space $C(R^n)$, where $R^n$ is an $n$-dimensional region, then there exists a map that functions as an isomorphism in a way that the relationship between the ratios of the norms of corresponding functions lies within a fixed range dependent on the dimensionality.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex atmospheric escape history, examining options for escape flux evolution and their implications for the atmosphere's chemical composition. We then examine the atmosphere's mid-term and short-term evolution, including the breakdown of low- to mid-density CO2 atmospheres and their observability. We discuss the atmosphere's interior-atmosphere and surface feedback loops, including the destruction of the magnetic field's influence, the oxidation of atmospheric components, and the consequences of cloud chemistry, as well as the breakdown of plate tectonics, the role of the core, and the mantle's influence. We summarize the atmosphere's evolutionary models and present equations to describe the long- and mid-term atmosphere's development, including the effect of the atmosphere's impact on the planet's surface and interior.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal firings, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters from a unidirectional record of events. We have established a Bayesian framework, developed the posterior inference using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, and compared it to variational approximations. Additionally, we have investigated the model's ability to generalize using cross-validation.

As high-power laser pulse parameters increase, nonlinear optical components must be reconfigured to accommodate them. We have developed a plasma waveplate that can emulates the axes of traditional crystal waveplates using a 3D emulated grid scattering network, providing a continuous and dynamic dispersion pattern. Our findings indicate that this plate can emulates the functions of both half and quarter crystal waveplates at a 225-GW/cm^2, 800-nm laser resonance frequency, with reflected energy reaching nearly 99% of the input. The ability to dynamically adjust polarization transformation is exhibited by this plate, with the ability to precisely control the output polarization state of linearly polarized light at a specific wavelength, even at a resonance frequency of 20-HW/cm^2. Due to its capacity to handle high-energy laser pulses with femtosecond duration, this plate has numerous potential scientific research, medical, and industrial applications.

Re-examining the search for a nonzero electric dipole moment (EDM) form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, in $\tau^+\tau^-$ production via $e^+ e^-$ collisions between the $\tau$-pair threshold and $\sqrt{s} \sim 15$ GeV is considered. The expected sensitivity to $d_\tau$ in the scenario where both produced $\tau$ leptons decay semihadronically is also investigated, reaching $\sim 1 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm/GeV$^2$ at $\sqrt{s} = 10.58$ GeV with the BABAR detector. Furthermore, improved options for reaching $\sim  few \times 10^{-21}$ e cm/GeV$^2$ at $\sqrt{s} = 80-120$ GeV with the CLIC and ILC projects are outlined, outperforming the optimal $\sim 3 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm/GeV$^2$ reach with the 100 GeV upgrade to the FCC-ee. The $\tau$ EDM search form factor is found to be closely related to the anomalous magnetic and electric dipole moments of the muon, with $\sim 0.1-10$ times better sensitivity than the best current forecasts for the muon anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\mu$, from

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code family comes with an efficient algorithm for determining codewords, enabling a distance of $2R(n+d)/d$ for an $(n,d)$ code capacity. Secondly, we investigate a specific code construction proposed by Gabidulin, demonstrating its capability to decode symmetric errors up to a certain capacity with an associated complexity of $O(n \log^{n-1} p)$ operations.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 4 up to day 400 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, was found to be unusually faint based on its SN~2018ho-like spectrum. However, this classification may be misleading since the strong absorption seen in the optical and UV spectra could be obscuring the true nature of SN~2020jfo. By integrating the luminosity of its SN~2018ho-like emission lines, we determined that SN~2020jfo actually belongs to the more intrinsically luminous short-period Type IIP supernovae. Based on its SN~2018ho-like characteristics, we estimated the mass of SN~2020jfo's progenitor to be between 9.5 and 12 times that of the Sun.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field in non-linear structure formation, regardless of the underlying cosmological parameters.

We have developed a novel approach to achieving equilibrium configurations for rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, based on a continuous Lagrangian formulation, utilizes a specific action as its foundation. By determining the action's stationary paths, we can derive the star's equations of motion. This allows us to directly manipulate a rotating fluid's configuration through small changes in radial and angular positions. When applied to axisymmetric configurations, this Lagrangian formulation results in equilibrium equations that are equivalent to those obtained through standard methods.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have identified the same number of distinct events resulting from compact binary mergers: gravitational waves generated by binary black hole collisions, binary neutron star collisions, and combinations of these collisions. To fully comprehend the properties of electromagnetic emissions from these collisions, it is crucial to detect and localize the associated source in the electromagnetic spectrum. The LIGO-Virgo collaborations anticipate the continued detection of such events in the future. The purpose of this review is to summarize the prospects for multi-messenger astronomy involving electromagnetic observations of these collisions from the present time until the upcoming decade, taking into consideration both past observations and collisions that may leave no electromagnetic signatures. Past observations of electromagnetic signals from these collisions, their frequencies, emission mechanisms, and associated astronomy are discussed in detail. The analysis also considers scenarios where neutron star mergers always produce gravitational waves, always result in the formation of a neutron star, or always merge without any electromagnetic signatures, in which case present and future capabilities for telescopes would either be sufficient or would need to be upgraded. The study also explores present and potential future telescopes for visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray, and radio wavelengths of light. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset from 4.3 million Google Photos to map global residential mobility patterns over a four-year period, from 2019 to 2022. By analyzing this data, researchers identified a distinct shift in staying home during the afternoon in 2022 compared to 2019, particularly in densely populated areas. This behavior suggests possible decreases in workplace diversity and potentially impacts economic outcomes such as innovation and income levels. A supplementary dataset from Pexels.com is additionally presented to support the main findings.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects can produce different effects, such as mergers rather than bursts, and object disruptions that could result in super-Eddington outflows affecting their surroundings.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the safe navigation of indoor environments with a mobile robot through a combination of conventional depth data and surface reflection analysis. By integrating the Ray Casting Approach with training datasets, we have produced synthetic training data to guide the model. The model integrates standard depth information with features related to material types, offered by analysis of reflection patterns, to identify areas of potential risk along planned routes and adjust the route to a safer path within the indoor environment. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating knowledge of surface reflection patterns in complex, changeable indoor settings leads to more accurate risk assessment and navigation in a variety of scenarios.

The prevalence of false news is deceivingly persuasive, with credible sources like NASA and CNN having their facts presented incorrectly, so it's crucial to understand the origin and spread of such misinformation. Although previous studies have highlighted the potential for misinformation to flourish in online news feeds, the impact of misinformation specifically spread through Twitter has largely been unexamined. To address this gap, we manually analyzed 200 falsely presented tweets that were directed at an online community of members in a massive mass membership organization. By examining the content of these tweets, we found that the primary motivation behind creating such misinformation appears to be malice rather than political or religious gain. Furthermore, we found that these tweets were often shared with the intention of embarrassing their targets, rather than for personal or ideological reasons. By hearing the voices of ordinary people behind the dissemination of misinformation, our findings hold significant implications for developing effective countermeasures to combat the spread of such misinformation.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with identical annotations. We subsequently utilize this metric to refine the existing annotations. A comparative analysis reveals that this approach outperforms random annotation updates and demonstrates a significant correlation with manual verification.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide the robot towards unexplored areas. To achieve this, a refined gradient-based approach is introduced, resulting in a tangent map that aids in navigation. The hiTMap framework's effectiveness has been demonstrated through simulation-based evaluations and a real-world demonstration.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices has historically been constrained by programming complexity and limited object-oriented capabilities. However, an emerging technique called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) has demonstrated superior performance in large-scale simulations and data processing tasks. We have developed an advanced SMMO framework called TOSCA, designed for 1D, 2D, and 3D object sets that efficiently utilizes SIMD instruction set extensions for enhanced speed. TOSCA features an innovative data structure called Method Packet, which groups related object data and method instructions to minimize overhead and prevent cache misses. By doing so, TOSCA achieves remarkable performance gains, such as a 1.7 to 5.5-fold increase in speed for C++-based CSD and CHASE algorithms when applied to 3D datasets exceeding 10 million entries. TOSCA's exceptional efficiency makes it an ideal platform for creating high-speed algorithms for O(n) and dynamic bit-vector management methods.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a 1-$d$ configuration splitting was found to be caused by the strong localization of the $d$-shell. In the case of the Mn domer, the YSR state splitting behavior was explained by the interplay between the two different YSR bands.

The NASA-ESA Telescopes for the Euclid Mission and James Webb Joint Transiting Exoplanet Survey (JWST-ETM) will provide in-depth analyses of the most detailed evolutionary data available for young planets. To achieve a comprehensive understanding of low-mexson exoplanets through secondary emission using next-generation ground and space-based telescopes like Euclid and JWST, precise sub-percent level knowledge of system star properties is necessary. The ETM project aims to create a catalog of exoplanet systems for observation using Transiting Exoplanet Survey Telescope (TESS) data, offering a vast array of potential targets for follow-up studies. This project will generate lists of the most informative current and future TESS observations of existing exoplanet systems. By applying TESS light curves and known rotation periods from TESS to the external data of a planet's system, Euclid can determine the optimal filter for follow-up observations to maximize the exoplanet signal detection. By incorporating these light curve characteristics and rotation periods, we can predict the most appropriate filter for Euclid-JWST observations to achieve a significant gain in signal-to-noise ratio. This approach will provide a substantial increase in the probability of successfully detecting a exoplanet's atmosphere.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  Calculations revealed that pristine TiO2 possesses wide-band gaps of approximately 3.51 eV and low liechtenstein - scuseria - benedictti corrections of 0.85 eV.  Both carbon and nitrogen defects are capable of dopant-like behavior, capable of introducing magnetic properties when present individually.  Specifically, substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects possess 0.35 $\mu$B and 1.05 $\mu$B of local magnetic moments respectively, residing primarily in neighboring titanium d-orbitals.  Covalent bonding between the defects and surrounding titanium atoms is a key contributor to these properties.  However, metallic behavior emerges when these defects form interstitial bonds.  A deep defect level associated with nitrogen exists near the bands' edge, hindering its ability to act as an effective n-type dopant.  Furthermore, we found UV absorption is caused by the defect-to-electron transition in both carbon and nitrogen defects.

This letter describes the demonstration of the ability to identify top-quark pairs produced in collisions at the Large Hadron Collider through the detection of protons deflected ahead of them. This achievement relies on precise measurements of the b-jet associated with the top-quark pair, which has a specific momentum range. The measurement of this associated particle, called a tag, is based on detailed simulations of its interaction and actual data from previous experiments. It validates the feasibility of utilizing two tagged particles, called taggers, to identify this rare event where the particle, called a remnant, emits a high-energy parton that becomes a flat, wide-component of the top-quark pair system. The result indicates that such a component constitutes less than 10% of the remaining particles associated with the top-quark pair system, which must be accounted for in future research where most of the particle's energy is in low-energy jets.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations with qudits outperform those with qubits. When it comes to achieving a fixed precision of 2 significant figures, it is evident that qudits outperform qubits, whether the noise level is varied or the system's size is expanded from $L=4$ to $L=8$. When it comes to mass density qudits have an advantage over qubits by a factor of 10 for errors produced from the Fermi-Dirac portal.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the extensive polarization of these positrons makes them suitable for a variety of fundamental and practical applications, including the investigation of spin-based effects in general relativity and particle-antiparticle mass comparisons. Although the polarization levels are predicted to be high, the existing theoretical models lack the accuracy to address this issue within the most effective parameter ranges, primarily due to deficiencies in strong-field qed numerics, in particular, the influence of the polarization of photons generated in the interaction. Our study overcomes these limitations through supercomputer-based simulations, providing a precise assessment of the polarization degrees by taking into account the intrinsic properties of the generated photons' spins. Our analysis reveals that the resulting polarization levels can vary significantly, as a result of the positrons' preferred emission angles and energies.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to the identity, and consequently, they possess a structured chain of nested subsets with a limited number of intermediate stages. This is associated with a newly discovered property, den as ϱ(S), which is related to a previously established property known as Grobner diameter, and it holds that groups with a polynomial diameter also have a related property ρ(S) that is slightly larger, and these two properties collectively constitute a hybrid framework. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and a compact size of 0.05$mm^2$. Experimental results demonstrate outstanding performance, including a 0.18{\deg}C resolution, a 0.6{\deg}C max error, and a 2.9mW power consumption at a -40{\deg}C temperature.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids. Building on the foundations laid out by Prangoski and Saorin, we extend their work on $G$-principal bundles over Lie groupoids to incorporate connections in terms of Lie algebra valued forms, demonstrating the chordate nature of resulting forms. Furthermore, we generalize the results from [PrS] concerning the surjectivity of the Chern-Weil map for closed forms, utilizing the approach introduced in [Mor].

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. This rule is supported by numerical simulations and shows strong correlation with simulation data. High-speed observations and stress recordings during the stick-slip regime reveal complex dynamics characterized by intermittent stress spikes, sudden film breaks, and oscillating patterns.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal forces, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computations reveal that inner-outer fluid arrangements, as well as the membrane's pre-stress state, influence the critical rotation speed at which the membrane starts to form a single, centrally positioned finger. Notably, near the point of instability, a sudden shift in finger placement from the periphery to the center occurs, accompanied by a corresponding change in scaling between finger size and overhanging fluid density.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible pathway for this detection involves a reaction with molecular hydrogen by the C5H5 radical. The observed ethynyl group in cyclopentadiene and cyclopentadiyne suggests a relatively high column density for this component. The absence of detected carbonyl counterparts to cyclopentadiyne points to a cycloaddition reaction being a primary pathway for cyclopentadiyne degradation. The cyclopropyl group in cyclopropylacetylene may have originated from the cyclopropyl radical combined with acetylene or the C3H radical with ethyne. The discrepancy between the cyclopropylacetylene and cyclopropyl cyclopropyne abundances suggests a difference in the prevalence of the cyclopropyl and C3H precursors.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically approaching these limits. A continuous and monotonic function of the phugoid field is used to describe the variation of the Hubble parameter, in order to facilitate the unified dark fluid model's classification and analysis. A specific function of this field has been introduced to ensure the model's theoretical consistency. Furthermore, a non-adimensional parameter has been defined to analyze the model's behavior in the presence of viscosity. This model has been found to successfully represent the universe's expansion history, by asymptotically matching the low and high energy regimes of the $\Lambda$CDM model. It has also been observed that the non-ad-dimensional parameter indicates when the model asymptotically converges to the $\Lambda$CDM regime. This has been supported by the fact that the dark energy density, pressure, and effective equation of state all exhibit the same parameter behavior. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we focus on light weakly interacting massive particles and sterile neutrinos, with an emphasis on dark matter. To accurately model the J/ψ decay process and associated backgrounds, we created a dedicated Monte Carlo tool. Our analysis of the J/ψ → invisible data provides stringent constraints on light sterile neutrinos and dark matter.
